transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 10:00 AM PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Cole (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Lunaris Head of ML), Mateo Ruiz (Lunaris Infra), Sarah Chen (Lunaris PM)
Shared artifacts: cost spreadsheet (link), benchmark results sheet (link), latency traces (link)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for squeezing this in. quick agenda — run through the latest cost/throughput numbers we ran last week, dig into caching and batching tradeoffs, then agree next steps. sound good?
[00:14] Priya: yep that works, thanks jordan. excited to see the numbers, we've been curious about the int8 run.
[00:20] Maya: cool — i'll kick us off with the numbers i put in the sheet. quick context: we ran three main configs on your sample prompt set (the 10k sample priya shared): hosted baseline, dedicated fp16, and dedicated int8 with prefix/KV cache enabled. also measured a few batching windows (1, 16, 64).
[00:34] Mateo: and you ran those against our dev dataset right, not production traffic?
[00:38] Maya: correct, dev sample only.
[00:40] Maya: hosted baseline — end-to-end we observed roughly 250-320 tokens/sec/$ (this is our internal tokens-per-dollar metric that factors in service overhead). p95 latency was around 180-220ms for single-request flows.
[00:55] Maya: dedicated fp16 — throughput improved to ~540 tokens/sec/$ with p95 at ~240ms.
[01:02] Maya: dedicated int8 w/ prefix cache — this is the big win: raw tokens/sec jumped to ~950-1,100 tokens/sec/$ depending on batching, and we saw a ~30-40% reduction in total token counts thanks to prefix caching for repeated system prompts and common prefixes in your dataset. p95 latency depends on batch size — single-request p95 was ~210ms, batch=64 pushed p95 up to ~600-700ms.
[01:25] Priya: that 30-40% token reduction — is that counting just prefix/KV cache hits or also response-level caching?
[01:31] Maya: primarily prefix/KV cache hits for autoregressive decode (we cached model KV states for common prefixes + rerank prompts). response caching for exact identical requests was minimal in your set. most savings came from repeated prefixes and multi-turn conversations where the beginning is identical.
[01:46] Sarah: can you explain how that translates to our tokens/sec/$? i want to understand the business impact.
[01:51] Jordan: sure — think of tokens/sec/$ as a normalized throughput metric: how many tokens the system can generate per dollar of infra/serving cost. so if int8 + caching yields 1,000 tokens/sec/$ vs hosted 300 tokens/sec/$, that means roughly 3x better unit economics for the same workload pattern.
[02:10] Mateo: are those numbers sensitive to seq length? our 95th pct for user messages is 420 tokens — will that change the comparatives?
[02:17] Maya: yes, sequence length matters. our tests here were weighted to your distribution — average seq ~120, 95th ~420. with heavier long-tail sequences the absolute tokens/sec/$ drops, but the relative improvement from int8+caching remains similar (20-35% uplift over fp16).
[02:34] Priya: about batching — you said batch=64 improved raw throughput, but p95 latency jumped. can you quantify the throughput gain?
[02:41] Maya: batch=64 gave ~2.2-2.6x raw tokens/sec compared to batch=1 on dedicated, but because you wait to fill the batch, end-to-end p95 can jump from ~210ms to ~600-700ms. for our customer interactive use-case we recommend staying under batch=16 for conversational endpoints if you care about p95 latency under 500ms.
[03:02] Jordan: to add — you can split workloads by policy: route low-latency interactive traffic to small-batch or cached paths, and route high-throughput async jobs (summarization, bulk inference) to larger batches on dedicated capacity. that's where smart routing helps.
[03:16] Mateo: how much does quantization impact quality? priya's worried about hallucination drift.
[03:20] Maya: good question — in our evals, int8 quantization (with per-channel calibration) had <2% delta on our BLEU/ROUGE-style and a small increase in off-by-one token errors on some prompts. we recommend holding quality checks in your eval harness; we can run A/B on a few critical prompts. priya?
[03:39] Priya: yes we'll need the A/B. quality is the primary gating for us, cost is secondary but important.
[03:44] Jordan: totally — that's why we propose the targeted prefix-cache benchmark next (Maya will run). we'll produce a csv with tokens generated, cache hit rates, p50/p95 latencies, and tokens/sec/$ so you can plug into your finance model.
[03:58] Sarah: on security — mat eo says they need KMS and audit logs details before we talk about committed capacity. mateo, do you want to elaborate?
[04:06] Mateo: yeah, for enterprise we'll need to confirm we can use our KMS, that logs hit our SIEM, and that there are RBAC controls. also audit retention windows.
[04:15] Jordan: understood — we'll coordinate a security deep-dive next week. jordan to schedule, and we'll bring our security solutions architect. (laughs)
[04:22] Priya: quick question on routing: if we pin a model version and one region gets saturated, can we failover to a quantized variant in another region automatically?
[04:31] Maya: yes — the routing layer supports fallback policies. we can define a compatible model family (eg fp16 -> int8) and route by latency/cost/region. the only caveat is cross-region adds egress latency, so perf characteristics will change.
[04:42] Priya: good to know.
[04:44] Jordan: ok recap and next steps — maya will run the prefix/KV benchmark on your 10k sample with batch sizes 1/16/64 and int8/fp16 configs, share the spreadsheet by 2026-03-11. jordan will send an updated cost/pricing spreadsheet that includes tokens/sec/$ math by 2026-03-06. mateo to whitelist test IPs by 2026-03-08. priya to share any additional high-priority prompts and confirm quality gating criteria by 2026-03-09. we'll schedule security deep-dive for next week.
[05:18] Priya: sounds good. one last thing — can you add a column that shows "cost per 1M effective tokens" after caching? that will make it easier for finance.
[05:26] Jordan: yes we'll add effective tokens and effective cost columns.
[05:29] Sarah: thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity.
[05:32] Jordan: thanks all — we'll follow up with the sheet and benchmark links. talk next week.

Transcript notes: occasional microphone clicks and overlap; some transcription errors expected (proper nouns like "KV cache" sometimes written as "kay vee").
